newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Montenegr PM keeps post despite Serbian pressure.
newsitem.headline: Montenegr PM keeps post despite Serbian pressure.

text.p: Montenegrin Prime Minister Milo Djukanovic on Friday survived attempts to force him from power for his attacks on Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, but Serbian leaders kept up their pressure for his removal.

The dispute has pitted pragmatists anxious to end Yugoslavia's international isolation against a socialist old guard grouped round Milosevic which is responding with reluctance to Western pressure for political reform.
Djukanovic roused hardliners' ire by demanding Milosevic's withdrawal from any political role in Yugoslavia's future and by courting support abroad.
A Montenegrin government session which ended early on Friday maintained Djukanovic in office and made no statement about three other ministers whose sacking had been sought.
But it stressed a commitment to Yugoslavia and brushed aside charges by pro-Serbia hardliners that it was pursuing a separatist policy.
In a conciliatory gesture, the government said it has accepted the resignation of its trade representative in Washington, Ratko Knezevic.
Serbian Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic returned immediately to the offensive and urged the Montenegrin parliament to dismiss Djukanovic as premier.

The ruling Montengrin Socialist party (DPS) Main Board on Monday forced Djukanovic to resign from a top party post and demanded that he dump his most trusted cabinet allies over his criticism of Milosevic.

Djukanovic said in an interview last month that Yugoslavia had no future with a man like Milosevic at its helm, prompting Belgrade to accuse him of seeking Montenegro's seccession from what remains of Yugoslavia.
Montenegro, Serbia's only partner in the federation and its only access to the sea, has been frustrated by the slow pace of reforms and conservative policies of its bigger alliy.
Djukanovic has pursued an open door policy to the West in contrast to Belgrade, which is isolated by an outer wall of sanctions and faces Western pressure over human rights.
Belgrade has interpreted Djukanovic's criticism of Milosevic as veiled separatism and pressed Bulatovic to oust the charismatic 35-year old politician. Djukanovic denies the charges.
Djukanovic enjoys widespread support including the liberal and popular speaker of the Montenegrin parliament, Svetozar Marovic, and most opposition parties.
He is applauded for his success in placing up to 95 percent of Montenegro's economy in private hands. Milosevic's Serbia has not even embarked on the privatisation road.
Hours later of Friday thousands rallied in Podgorica in support of Djukanovic, venting anger at Milosevic for the first time since the Serbian president came to power 10 years ago.

"We are not defending Montenegro from Serbia but from the fascist regime of Slobodan Milosevic and his wife" said Bozidar Bogdanovic before the newly-formed Democratic Movement for Montenegro which organised the rally.
"It is high time for the Montenegrin people to stand up in defence of Montenegro and its dignity," said Bogdanovic.
"Let us stand for democratic and prosperous Montenegro and Yugoslavia against Milosevic's unitarism," said Slobodan Curovic an art school student from Cetinje.
